meta.blurb: Four sisters, one small house and a war far away. Meg, Jo, Beth and Amy grow up in the March family, learning about love, loss and following their dreams. Louisa May Alcott's beloved story of home, retold for learners.
meta.bible: Meg March (Margaret): the eldest sister, pretty and gentle; she marries John Brooke. Jo March (Josephine): the second sister, a writer, tomboyish and quick-tempered; she marries Professor Bhaer. Beth March (Elizabeth): the third sister, shy, musical and kind; she dies young after illness. Amy March: the youngest sister, an artist who likes fine things; she marries Laurie. Marmee (Mrs March): the wise, loving mother. Mr March: the father, a chaplain with the army in the American Civil War, who comes home at the end of the first part. Aunt March: a rich, sharp-tongued relative. Hannah: the March family's faithful servant. Theodore Laurence: called Laurie, the lively boy next door; he loves Jo, but she says no. Mr Laurence: Laurie's kind grandfather, who gives Beth a piano. John Brooke: Laurie's tutor, who marries Meg. Daisy and Demi: Meg's twin children. Professor Friedrich Bhaer: a kind German teacher in New York, called Fritz by Jo. Mrs Kirke: the owner of the boarding house in New York. Aunt Carrol: the relative who takes Amy to Europe. The Hummels: a poor family near the Marches. Sallie Gardiner and Annie Moffat: friends of Meg. Fred Vaughn: a rich young man who courts Amy. Rob and Teddy: Jo's two young sons. Concord: the town in Massachusetts where the Marches live. New York: where Jo works as a governess. Plumfield: the big house Jo inherits from Aunt March. Europe: where Amy travels. Nice: the French seaside city where Amy and Laurie meet. Fixed facts: the story begins one Christmas during the American Civil War; Beth dies in the second part; Jo refuses Laurie, who marries Amy; Jo and Professor Bhaer marry and open a school at Plumfield. Voice and tone: warm, homely, humorous and moral, with gentle sadness; illness and death are told plainly and kindly.

B1B2: It is the week before Christmas, and the four March sisters are sitting by the fire. They complain that Christmas will not be Christmas without presents, because the war has made them poor.

Their mother, whom the girls call Marmee, comes in with a letter from their father, who is serving as a chaplain in the army. He sends his love and asks them to be good, so the girls promise to try harder.

On Christmas morning, Marmee asks the girls to give their breakfast to the Hummels, a poor family with a sick baby and many hungry children. They carry it through the snow, and it makes them happier than any gift could.
That night Jo's play is performed in the attic, and the sisters wear paper crowns and old costumes. When they return to the house, a rich neighbour has sent them a wonderful supper with ice cream.
At a New Year's party, Jo hides behind a curtain because she has burned the back of her dress. There she meets a tall boy, Laurie, who lives in the big house next door.
Laurie is lonely in his grandfather's big house, and he has watched the March sisters through their window. Soon he is a daily visitor, and Marmee tells him he may think of her as a second mother.
Beth is too shy to speak to old Mr Laurence, but she loves music and cannot stay away from his piano. He is so touched by her playing that he gives her the piano as a present.

Amy is very fond of pickled limes, which are forbidden at school, and she brings some to class. When her teacher finds out, he punishes her in front of everyone, and Marmee takes her out of the school.

Amy is angry because Jo did not take her to the theatre, and in revenge she burns Jo's book of stories. When Amy later falls through the thin ice, Jo has to help save her, and she learns to control her temper.
Meg spends two weeks with her rich friend Annie Moffat and wishes that she had fine clothes like the other girls. They dress her in a borrowed gown and curl her hair, and she looks like a doll.
Meg is unhappy because she listened to unkind gossip, and she confesses everything to Marmee. Her mother tells her that love and honest work are worth far more than money and parties.
The sisters make a family newspaper and call it the Pickwick Club, and Laurie asks to join in. He puts funny letters in a post box in the garden wall, and the whole family laughs.
Meg and Jo decide to do no work for a whole week, and Marmee lets them try. By Saturday the house is untidy, the meals are bad, and they are all very unhappy.
Laurie invites the March girls to a camp by the river, where he has English friends. Meg is shy with Laurie's tutor, John Brooke, who is quiet and kind.

One afternoon the sisters talk about their dreams, which they call castles in the air. Meg wants a lovely home, Jo wants to write books, Beth wants everyone to be well and Amy wants to be a great artist.

A telegram comes to say that Father is very ill in a Washington hospital and Marmee must go to him at once. The family has little money, so Jo cuts off her beautiful hair and sells it for twenty-five dollars.
While their mother is away, the sisters try to be good, and Beth goes on visiting the Hummels. The Hummel baby dies of scarlet fever, and Beth catches the illness herself.
Beth grows so ill that she does not know her family, and Amy is sent to stay with Aunt March. Jo nurses her sister night and day, and Laurie sends a telegram to bring Marmee home.
Just before dawn, the fever breaks, and Beth falls into a peaceful sleep. Marmee arrives at the house a few hours later, and the girls rush to hug her.
One snowy Christmas, Mr March comes home from the war, and his family is together again. Beth, still weak, sits in his arms, and Meg blushes when she sees Mr Brooke.
Mr Brooke has fallen in love with Meg, who is not yet sure of her heart. Jo is very upset because she wants her family to stay together and does not want to lose a sister.
Aunt March says that she will not give any money to Meg if she marries a poor man. Meg says that she is happy to marry John Brooke because she loves him, and she will work hard beside him.
Three years later the war has ended, and Meg marries John Brooke in the March family's garden. She wears a simple white dress and wants no show, because she is marrying for love.
In her new little house, Meg tries to make currant jelly and fails completely. She cries when John comes home with a guest, and the dinner is not ready.
After a quarrel about money, Meg and John do not speak for a day. Marmee tells Meg that a wife must be patient, and the young couple forgive each other.
Meg has twin babies, a girl called Daisy and a boy called Demi, and they keep her busy day and night. She becomes so tired that John begins to spend his evenings away from home.
Jo spends her days in the attic, writing stories as fast as she can. A newspaper pays her for several exciting tales, and she is proud to help her family with the money.
Their relative Aunt Carrol plans a trip to Europe, and Aunt March decides which sister should go. She chooses Amy because Amy has better manners, and Jo must stay at home.
Jo wants to earn her own living, so she goes to New York to teach two small girls. She stays in a boarding house run by Mrs Kirke and writes stories at night.
At the boarding house, Jo meets Professor Bhaer, a kind German teacher who is poor but cheerful. He teaches her some German, and in return she mends his old socks.
Professor Bhaer reads one of Jo's thrilling stories in the newspaper and says gently that she can do better. Jo is hurt at first, but she knows that he is right.
A letter from home says that Beth is ill again, and Jo returns to Concord. Professor Bhaer comes to say goodbye to her, and she feels a little sad.
Laurie has finished college, and he asks Jo to marry him. She tells him that she loves him as a dear friend, but she cannot love him as a husband.
Laurie is so unhappy that his grandfather takes him on a long journey to Europe. Jo is very sad to lose her best friend, but she knows she was right to say no.
Beth is very weak, and the doctor says that she may not live long. At the seaside, she tells Jo quietly that she knows she will not get well.
Beth is brought home, and she is cared for by the whole family. In the early spring she dies peacefully, with her mother and sisters beside her.
After Beth dies, Jo is lonely and sad, and she sees her father and mother growing older. She decides to stay at home, to be a good daughter and to write stories for them.
In Europe, Amy hears the sad news that Beth has died, and she is very lonely. Laurie, who has just learned the news too, sits with her and finds that he loves her.
In Europe, Amy meets Laurie again, and he seems lazy and unhappy. She tells him that he should work hard and make something of himself, and he listens to her.
Laurie and Amy spend many happy days together in Europe, and he finds that he has forgotten his old pain. He asks Amy to marry him on a quiet lake, and she says yes.
Jo is happy for her sisters, but she feels lonely in the quiet house. Marmee tells her that love will come in time and that she should not be afraid of it.
One rainy afternoon Professor Bhaer knocks at the door of the March house. The whole family welcomes him, and Mr March likes the kind professor at once.
Professor Bhaer says that he must go west to teach, and he and Jo walk together in the rain. Under one umbrella, he tells her that he loves her, and she says that she loves him too.
Aunt March dies suddenly, and to everyone's surprise she leaves her large house, Plumfield, to Jo. Jo and Professor Bhaer are now free to plan their future together.
Jo and Professor Bhaer marry, and they decide to open a school for boys at Plumfield. Jo is delighted to have so many children to care for.
Plumfield is soon full of boys who play in the garden and learn their lessons. Jo has little time to write, but she has two little sons of her own, Rob and Teddy.
It is Marmee's sixtieth birthday, and the whole family comes to Plumfield to pick apples. Meg, John, Daisy and Demi come, and so do Jo's boys and the old Mr March.
They sit at a long table in the garden and eat a big meal. The boys give Marmee a gift, and she is so touched that she cannot speak.
Marmee says that she has never felt happier and that she has everything she wants. Jo looks around at her family and thinks that her castle in the air has become real.
In the evening, the visitors go home, and the house becomes quiet again. Jo thinks of Beth and feels that she is still near, and she is peaceful.
C1C2: On a cold December evening in Concord, the four March sisters gathered around the fire, grumbling that Christmas would be no Christmas without presents. Meg, the eldest, longed for pretty clothes, Jo for books, Beth for a piano, and Amy for drawing pencils. Yet, as they spoke, they remembered that their father was far away with the army, and a quiet came over the room.

Their mother, whom they affectionately called Marmee, came home with a letter from Mr March, who was serving as a chaplain with the Union army. He wrote tenderly of his longing to see them again and asked them to use the winter to become little women, worthy of the welcome he hoped to give. Each sister, with tears glistening in her eyes, silently resolved to be gentler, more patient and more useful in the months that lay ahead.

On Christmas morning, Marmee told her daughters about the Hummels, a poor German family near by, who had no fire and no breakfast, and asked whether they would carry their own to them. The sisters wrapped up warmly and trudged through the snow with muffins, bread and milk, and the sight of the hungry children eating filled them with a joy they had not expected. That Christmas morning, on their return to their own small parlour, they were more truly grateful for their warm fire and plain home than for any gift.

That evening, the sisters performed a melodrama that Jo had written, with paper crowns, old curtains and a great deal of shouting, and the small audience of friends laughed until they cried. When the sisters returned to the parlour afterwards, they found a magnificent supper of ice cream, cake and fruit, sent over by old Mr Laurence, their rich neighbour. After a year of anxious economy, the unexpected luxury seemed almost too wonderful to be real, and the sisters could scarcely believe their luck.

At a party on New Year's Eve, Jo hid in an alcove behind a curtain, anxious to conceal a scorch mark on the back of her only good dress. There she met the grandson of old Mr Laurence, a lively, dark-eyed boy named Laurie, who also hated crowds and was glad of company. A friendship that began in awkward confusion over a scorched dress, and a shared dislike of the crowd, was to last for many years afterwards.

Laurie, who lived a lonely life in his grandfather's grand house, had long watched the cheerful March family through their window with something close to envy. Before long he was a daily visitor, delighting the sisters with his jokes and ideas, while Marmee, noticing his loneliness, welcomed him as if he were her own son. The house on the hill and the house next door were rapidly becoming one family.

Beth, who was frightened of nearly everyone, found her courage when old Mr Laurence invited her to play on the splendid piano that stood unused in his drawing room. He listened with such quiet kindness that she overcame her fear and returned each afternoon, until he sent a lovely little piano to the March house as a gift. In gratitude for his generosity, she stitched him a pair of slippers with her own hands, and the old gentleman treasured them as a priceless present.

Pickled limes were all the fashion among the girls at school, but Mr Davis, the teacher, had forbidden them, and Amy was caught with a pocketful. He punished her in front of the whole class, and she stood through the lesson with her face burning with shame and tears running down her cheeks. When she told Marmee at home, her mother withdrew her from the school at once.

Furious at being left behind on a theatre outing, Amy burned the precious book of stories that Jo had spent years writing, and Jo, who had a quick and violent temper, refused to forgive her. When Amy fell through thin ice on the river the next day, Jo was among the first to rescue her, and she was horrified to realise how close she had come to losing her sister. Marmee confessed that she too had a temper, which she had learned to master.

Meg spent a fortnight with her wealthy friend Annie Moffat, where the elegant dresses and silly chatter of the other girls made her ashamed of her own plain gowns. At a party, they dressed her in a borrowed silk dress, powdered her cheeks and curled her hair until she hardly knew herself in the mirror. Laurie, arriving, took one look and told her frankly that he did not like it.

Back at home, Meg confessed to Marmee that she had been dazzled by the Moffats' wealth and had even been foolish enough to listen to cruel gossip about her mother's plans. Marmee told her gently that she would rather see her daughters poor and happy than rich and discontented, and that a loving heart was worth more than any fine dress. Meg, relieved of her secret worry and ashamed of her vanity, felt as if a heavy weight had been lifted from her young shoulders.

The sisters founded a little club in the attic, with a weekly newspaper full of jokes, poems and stories, which they read aloud each Saturday night. Laurie, who had been asking to join, was at last admitted as a member and soon filled the old box in the garden wall with funny letters. The post office he invented was a secret between friends, and it was destined to carry far more than jokes.

Tired of chores, the sisters asked Marmee to let them do nothing for a week, and she cheerfully agreed, taking a holiday of her own. By Saturday the rooms were a muddle, the dinner was a disaster, the bird had died and everybody was bored and cross. Even Jo, who had resisted all the lessons and good advice, admitted that work, however tiresome, was a better companion than idleness and boredom.

On a bright summer day, Laurie invited the March girls to a picnic by the river, where he had asked a few English friends to join them. Meg took tea with Mr Brooke, the shy young tutor, who spoke warmly of Laurie and offered to read aloud, and she found herself unexpectedly happy. The others played games on the grass, and the long summer day drifted peacefully into evening, with the river turning gold beneath the setting sun.

One lazy afternoon the sisters lay in the hayloft and described their castles in the air, the dreams they hoped would one day come true. Meg wanted a beautiful home and a loving husband, Jo a shelf of famous books, Beth a safe house with her family, and Amy a career as a great painter in Rome. Laurie, who was listening beside them, found himself wondering where his own castle might one day stand and who would be inside it.

A telegram arrived, saying that Mr March lay gravely ill in a Washington hospital and asking Marmee to come at once. The family had too little money for the journey, so Jo, without a word of warning, went to a barber and sold her long chestnut hair for twenty-five dollars. When she came home with her head cropped like a boy's, she wept quietly in the dark.

Marmee left for Washington, and for a few weeks the girls bravely tried to keep the house in order, each helping where she could. Beth, who had always been the one to visit the Hummels, caught scarlet fever from the poor family's baby, which died in her arms. Soon she lay in bed with a burning fever and heavy eyes, hardly able to speak, while her sisters hovered anxiously around her.

Beth was soon so ill that she scarcely knew her own sisters, and to protect her from infection, Amy was sent to stay with the grumbling Aunt March. Jo nursed her through the long nights, praying for the first time in years with real fervour, while Laurie quietly sent a telegram to Marmee. The doctor said gravely that the coming night would decide everything, and the household sat up together, hardly daring to breathe or to hope.

Just before dawn, the fever broke, and Beth turned her head and slept peacefully for the first time in many days. A few hours later, Marmee arrived, tired from her journey, and the sisters crowded around her with tears and laughter. It was, as they all agreed afterwards, the best news they had ever received, and no other Christmas present could ever compare with it.

At Christmas the following year, Mr March returned from Washington, thinner and greyer, and his four daughters ran to meet him through the snow. Beth, still pale from her illness, was carried to a seat by the fire, and the family sat down at last to the happiest supper they could remember. Only Meg, glancing shyly at Mr Brooke across the room, blushed deeply and looked away, as though she feared that her thoughts might be read.

John Brooke, who had long admired Meg in silence, at last asked Mr March for permission to court his eldest daughter, and she was surprised to find herself trembling. Jo was horrified by the idea, since she hated the thought of any outsider carrying off her beloved sister, and she said so without much tact. Meg, however, listened with downcast eyes and a quiet smile, for she was already thrilled by the thought of being loved and chosen.

Aunt March, hearing of the romance, announced in a sharp voice that she would leave Meg nothing if she married a poor man and urged her to find a rich husband instead. Meg, who was gentle in most things, answered with surprising firmness that she loved John Brooke and would be glad to work beside him. Aunt March, left speechless with fury, swept out of the house, and Meg's happiness, unspoiled by the old lady's threats, only grew brighter.

Three years went by, the war ended, and John Brooke, who had found steady work, at last asked Meg to name the day. The wedding took place in the March family's parlour in June, with roses in the garden and no fine dress, because Meg said she wished to be married as herself. Jo, though secretly sad to lose her sister, helped at every step with a good grace, and she even managed to keep her tongue under control.

Eager to prove herself a good housekeeper, Meg decided to preserve a large batch of currant jelly, but the sticky red mixture simply refused to set, however long she boiled it. When John arrived unexpectedly with a guest for dinner, he found a messy kitchen, a weeping wife and no meal at all. For that miserable evening she felt as though her whole married life had begun with a disaster from which she might never recover.

Meg, who had spent too much money on silk for a dress, and John, who was too proud to tell her how much he worried, quarrelled bitterly over the matter. Marmee, hearing the story from her daughter, advised her to be patient and to listen to her husband, and to say she was sorry first. By evening, with Marmee's wise advice still ringing in her ears, the young couple had gladly forgiven one another and made peace over the table.

Soon Meg was the mother of twins, a quiet little girl named Daisy and a sturdy, curious boy named Demi, and she spent every hour taking care of them. In her devotion she began to neglect her husband, who found himself spending his evenings elsewhere, until Marmee reminded her that a husband also needs attention. After that, the little house grew quite peaceful, for the young mother learned to share her time between her children and the husband she loved.

In the attic, Jo wrote her stories for hours at a stretch, wearing her special writing cap and sustained only by apples and the hope of success. At last a newspaper paid her for several tales, and she was delighted, even though the stories were full of murders and mysteries that she was not proud of. The money she earned went straight to her family, and she felt a quiet pride in being able to help them, for the first time in her life.

When Aunt Carrol planned a long trip to Europe, it fell to Aunt March to decide which of her nieces should go, and she weighed Jo's blunt tongue against Amy's graceful manners. She chose Amy, who sailed delightedly away to see the pictures and palaces she had always dreamed of, and left Jo behind to swallow her disappointment. Jo, who could never quite hide her feelings, could not entirely disguise her tears, and she turned away so that no one would see her disappointment.

Restless at home, Jo decided to earn her own living and found a post in New York as a governess to the two small daughters of Mrs Kirke, who ran a boarding house. She was given a small room at the top of the house, where she wrote in the evenings and dreamed of success. For the first time in her life, she felt truly independent, free to rely on her own energy and to build a future entirely of her own making.

At the boarding house Jo met Professor Bhaer, a middle-aged German scholar who had come to America to teach, and who earned just enough to look after two orphaned nephews. He was shabbily dressed and shy about his English, but his goodness shone so brightly that all the children loved him. Jo, in return for his lessons in German, quietly mended his socks and sewed buttons on his coat, and he was touched by her thoughtfulness.

Professor Bhaer came across one of the lurid tales in the newspapers, and, though he did not know that Jo had written it, he said gravely that such stories were a poor use of any good mind. Jo defended herself at first, since she needed the money, but his gentle honesty made her feel ashamed. That night, with a sigh and a feeling of relief, she carried every one of them to the stove and watched them curl and crumble into ashes.

When she heard that Beth had become ill again, Jo packed her bags and prepared for the train home, determined to be at her sister's side. Professor Bhaer came to say goodbye, and she was surprised at how much she disliked leaving him behind. She told herself firmly, all the way home on the train, that she was only worried about Beth, and that nothing else was troubling her.

Laurie, who had graduated from college with honours, had waited years for the right moment, and at last he told Jo that he loved her and begged her to be his wife. Jo, though devoted to him as a brother, knew in her heart that they were too alike and would make each other unhappy. She refused him gently but firmly, and it grieved her deeply to watch the hope drain from the face of the boy who had been her dearest friend.

Laurie, deeply hurt, left at once for Europe with his grandfather, who hoped that travel would soothe his grandson's heart. Jo felt that she had lost her best friend, and though she knew that she could never have been happy as his wife, the house felt strangely empty without his cheerful whistle at the gate. She turned all her attention to Beth, determined to give her sister every comfort and every hour of the time that was left.

By now Beth was so frail that she could scarcely climb the stairs, and the doctor, after a long silence, told the family that she might not live very long. Jo took her to the seashore, where the two sisters sat together by the waves, and Beth said quietly that she knew she was not going to get better. Jo wept openly, unable to hide her fear, but Beth, calmer than anyone, comforted her and said that she was not afraid of what lay ahead.

Beth came home to the family, where she was cared for tenderly through the winter, and she spent her last months making small gifts for her friends. In the early spring she died peacefully, with Marmee and her sisters by her side, and it seemed to Jo that the whole house had lost its light. The family wept together for many days, but in the midst of their sorrow there was a sort of calm, as though Beth's gentle spirit still watched over them.

In the months after Beth's death, Jo sat alone in the attic, aching with grief, and she began to understand how much her parents needed her. She vowed to stay at home and be more patient, more gentle and more thoughtful, as Beth had always been, and her stories grew simpler and truer. Marmee watched her daughter with deep love and not a little pride, for she saw how bravely the girl was trying to grow into a better woman.

Far away in Europe, Amy received the black-edged letter that told her of Beth's death, and she wept as she had not wept since she was a child. Laurie, who had heard the same news in his own heart, comforted her quietly and tenderly, and as her sobs eased, the two realised that they now felt much more than friendship. The old grief, strangely and gently, had begun to turn to love, and neither of them could have said exactly when the change had begun.

Meanwhile in Europe, Amy met Laurie again, and found him lounging idly about, wasting his talent and his grandfather's money. She told him frankly that she was disappointed, and that a man of his gifts ought to make something of himself rather than pine for a girl who would not have him. He thought about her words for a long time in silence, and then, to his own surprise, he sat down at the piano and began to compose music again.

Over the following months, the two grew very close, and Laurie discovered to his surprise that the old ache for Jo had faded and that he loved the clever, graceful girl beside him. On a still afternoon, in a boat on a quiet lake, he asked Amy to be his wife, and she accepted with joy. They were married soon after in Europe, in a quiet ceremony with few guests, and they wrote at once to tell the family at home.

Jo, who was happy for her sisters but deeply lonely, sometimes wished that she could stay a child forever, and she confided in Marmee that she felt strangely empty. Her mother answered tenderly that many women have to find their own paths and that Jo's talents and her loving heart would not go unrewarded. Jo, comforted by her mother's wisdom and her tender patience, began slowly to look at the future with something close to hope instead of fear.

One rainy afternoon, as Jo sat musing in the parlour, the bell rang, and there stood Professor Bhaer on the doorstep, his hat in his hand and a smile on his face. Marmee welcomed him warmly, Mr March spoke with him for hours about philosophy, and the family saw at once that he was a good man. Jo, who had secretly hoped for exactly this visit for months, was suddenly overcome by shyness and stood speechless in the doorway for a long moment.

When the professor said that he must go west for a position, Jo felt a great sadness, and while walking with him in the rain, she found the courage to tell him that she wanted him to stay. Beneath the shelter of his umbrella, he told her that he was poor and had little to offer, and she said that she wanted nothing else but him. They were engaged on the spot, in the wet road, beneath the old umbrella, and neither of them noticed that the rain had drenched them both.

Aunt March died suddenly, and when her will was read, it was found that she had left Plumfield, her large old house, to Jo, who had so often tried her patience. Jo, who had never expected anything, and the professor, who was still working far away, now began to dream of what they might do with so spacious a home. At last the engaged couple, after so many months of patient waiting and small economies, had a real future and a home in which to build it.

In time Jo and Professor Bhaer were married, and they decided to fill the big house with boys, especially those with no one else to care for them. The idea was Jo's, and she was thrilled at the thought of so many bright faces, so many noisy meals and so much work, which was exactly what she liked. Her husband, whom she affectionately called Fritz, agreed with all his heart and offered to teach the boys everything he knew, from German to good manners.

In a few years Plumfield was full of boys, some rich, some poor, some mischievous and some meek, and the old house rang with their laughter and their quarrels. Jo found less time for writing, but she loved her work, and she was happy to be a mother to her own two sons, Rob and Teddy. Her husband's patient love and good sense, and his gift for understanding even the naughtiest boy, made the school succeed beyond all their hopes.

In the autumn, on Marmee's sixtieth birthday, the family gathered at Plumfield for an apple-picking, and the orchard was full of children, boys and grown-ups. Meg and John came with Daisy and Demi, Mr March sat in the sunshine, and Jo's boys swarmed up the trees, all of them laughing and glad. Everyone agreed, as the long golden afternoon wore on, that it was the happiest day they could remember, and that Marmee deserved all of it.

When the apples were picked, the whole company sat at a long table in the garden and shared a feast that the boys had helped to prepare. Then the children presented their gift to Marmee, and she, usually so calm, was so moved by the kindness that for a few moments she could not speak. Her eyes were bright with happy tears, and she thanked them all in a quiet voice that trembled just a little, which only made them love her more.

Marmee said, with a smile, that she had never in her life felt so happy and that all her daughters, married or not, had made her proud. Jo looked around at her family, at her husband, her boys and the old house full of laughter, and she realised that she had somehow built something far better than the castles she had once dreamed of. She was surprised, and a little amused, to discover how little she missed the old castles, now that she was living in something so much warmer.

As evening fell and the visitors went home, the house grew quiet again, and Jo sat for a moment on the porch, thinking of the sister who was no longer with them. She felt that Beth was still near, in the garden and the music and the kindness that lingered in the house, and her heart was full of peace. Then, with a last look at the darkening hills, she went inside, where her family was waiting, and the lamps were being lit one by one.
